title: Log-Concavity Genus Distribution Conjecture (LCGD Conjecture)
statement_text: The genus distribution of every graph is log-concave.
context_text: While computing embedding distributions of various infinite families of graphs, Gross, Robbins, and Tucker proposed this conjecture in 1989. It had been confirmed for many families including bouquets of loops, dipoles, graphs constructed by vertex and edge-amalgamations, linear sequences of graphs, ring-like families, and Halin graphs. The conjecture is reminiscent of the Heron–Rota–Welsh log-concavity conjecture and is related to $\Delta$-matroids and the Bollobás–Riordan polynomial.
paper_contribution: Disproves the LCGD Conjecture by providing explicit examples exhibiting strong deviation from log-concavity at multiple terms of their genus sequences (Theorems 3 and 9).

title: Conjecture 10
statement_text: The genus distribution of every graph $G$ is unimodal.
context_text: Graphs are connected and simple, and surfaces are closed orientable surfaces. The genus distribution (or genus sequence) of $G$ is the sequence $(a_g(G))_{g\ge0}$, where $a_g(G)$ is the number of 2-cell embeddings of $G$ in the orientable surface of genus $g$ (up to ambient homeomorphism). A sequence of non-negative numbers is log-concave if $a_k^2\ge a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$ for every $k\ge1$, and unimodal if it is non-decreasing up to some index and non-increasing afterwards (log-concave sequences without internal zeros are unimodal). Gross, Robbins and Tucker conjectured in 1989 (the LCGD Conjecture) that the genus distribution of every graph is log-concave; the author disproves it, showing that for every $g\ge0$ and $k\ge1$ there is a 4-connected graph of genus $g$ whose genus sequence has $k$ consecutive strictly log-convex terms. These counterexamples are still unimodal, and the author suggests that the unimodal weakening of the LCGD Conjecture could, and actually should, still be true. The author compares the LCGD Conjecture with the Heron–Rota–Welsh log-concavity conjecture for matroids, whose weaker unimodal form (Read's conjecture) was proved first by Huh, before the full conjecture was proved by Adiprasito, Huh and Katz.

title: Conjecture 11
statement_text: Every graph that triangulates some surface has log-concave genus distribution.
context_text: Graphs are connected and simple, and surfaces are closed orientable surfaces. The genus distribution (or genus sequence) of $G$ is the sequence $(a_g(G))_{g\ge0}$, where $a_g(G)$ is the number of 2-cell embeddings of $G$ in the orientable surface of genus $g$ (up to ambient homeomorphism). A sequence of non-negative numbers is log-concave if $a_k^2\ge a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$ for every $k\ge1$, and unimodal if it is non-decreasing up to some index and non-increasing afterwards (log-concave sequences without internal zeros are unimodal). Gross, Robbins and Tucker conjectured in 1989 (the LCGD Conjecture) that the genus distribution of every graph is log-concave; the author disproves it, showing that for every $g\ge0$ and $k\ge1$ there is a 4-connected graph of genus $g$ whose genus sequence has $k$ consecutive strictly log-convex terms. A graph triangulates a surface if it has a 2-cell embedding in that surface in which every face is a triangle. After proposing that every genus distribution is unimodal, the author notes that this restricted form of log-concavity also looks plausible.
